proposals.name: Curiosity gap
proposals.instruction: DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the headline makes the reader want a missing outcome or explanation while remaining understandable. Scores low when it states the complete takeaway or is merely opaque; does not apply without an implied information gap.
proposals.rationale: Clicking helps resolve an information gap while preserving enough context to make the gap intelligible.

proposals.name: Plain-language clarity
proposals.instruction: DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the subject, action, and meaning are immediately clear in ordinary language. Scores low when wording is ambiguous, compressed, or jargon-heavy; does not apply when the headline makes no substantive proposition.
proposals.rationale: Readership favors headlines that reduce processing effort and make the story immediately legible.

proposals.name: Emotional arousal
proposals.instruction: DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the headline conveys strong fear, anger, joy, tenderness, or disgust. Scores low when it is emotionally neutral; does not apply without a discernible emotional cue.
proposals.rationale: Strong emotions increase attention and sharing even when traditional news-value signals are weak.

proposals.name: Personal consequence
proposals.instruction: DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the subject plausibly affects an ordinary reader’s own health, safety, money, rights, or family. Scores low when consequences are remote or abstract; does not apply without a personal implication.
proposals.rationale: Readers prioritize stories affecting their lives, beyond aggregate economic or domestic significance.

proposals.name: Moral transgression
proposals.instruction: DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the headline presents taboo, betrayal, injustice, exploitation, or scandal. Scores low when it describes routine or norm-consistent behavior; does not apply without a clear conduct or norm signal.
proposals.rationale: Moral transgression invites judgment and discussion, generating interest beyond the presence of legal proceedings.

proposals.name: Interpersonal conflict
proposals.instruction: DESCRIPTION: Scores high when identifiable people or groups oppose, accuse, reject, or challenge one another. Scores low when relationships are cooperative or non-adversarial; does not apply without explicit antagonism.
proposals.rationale: Social contests attract follow-up attention even without crisis, violence, or institutional action.

proposals.name: Unresolved trajectory
proposals.instruction: DESCRIPTION: Scores high when a decision, result, threat, or consequence remains pending and invites monitoring. Scores low when the event and outcome are settled; does not apply without temporal progression.
proposals.rationale: Pending outcomes create a reason to click now and return for resolution.

proposals.name: Cultural touchstone
proposals.instruction: DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the headline invokes a widely recognizable cultural object, phrase, franchise, or shared reference. Scores low when the reference is obscure; does not apply without a cultural referent.
proposals.rationale: Shared references lower recognition costs and broaden the potential audience.

proposals.name: Explanatory promise
proposals.instruction: DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the wording promises to explain why, how, or what happened. Scores low when it merely announces an event; does not apply without an implied explanatory question.
proposals.rationale: Explanatory framing motivates information-seeking beyond simple event awareness.

proposals.name: Direct personal voice
proposals.instruction: DESCRIPTION: Scores high when a first-person admission, plea, testimony, or strongly voiced quotation is central. Scores low when the headline is impersonal summary; does not apply without a human speaker.
proposals.rationale: Direct voice supplies authenticity and emotional immediacy, strengthening reader engagement.

proposals.name: Humorous framing
proposals.instruction: DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the headline uses wit, wordplay, comic contrast, or playful absurdity. Scores low when its tone is strictly literal or formal; does not apply without a playful cue.
proposals.rationale: Playful framing can attract clicks despite low conventional news value.

proposals.name: Visual imaginability
proposals.instruction: DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the headline evokes a concrete scene, object, or action that is easy to picture. Scores low when it is abstract or bureaucratic; does not apply when it lacks concrete content.
proposals.rationale: Concrete imagery improves memorability and mental simulation, supporting spontaneous readership.

proposals.name: Actionable utility
proposals.instruction: DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the story appears to offer advice, protection, instructions, or decision-relevant information. Scores low when it offers no practical takeaway; does not apply without an implied action or choice.
proposals.rationale: Practical guidance gives readers immediate instrumental value, distinct from general interest.

proposals.name: Identity resonance
proposals.instruction: DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the headline invites identification with or judgment of a religious, ethnic, national, sexual, or political group. Scores low when it is socially impersonal; does not apply without an identity-bearing group.
proposals.rationale: Identity-relevant stories invite self-placement and group discussion beyond event magnitude.

proposals.name: Narrative coherence
proposals.instruction: DESCRIPTION: Scores high when the headline forms a compact story with an agent, action, and consequence or tension. Scores low when it is fragmentary, list-like, or overloaded; does not apply when too little content supports a narrative.
proposals.rationale: Coherent mini-narratives are easier to process and mentally complete, encouraging readers to enter the story.

proposals.name: Headline length band
proposals.instruction: DESCRIPTION: Count the words; mark yes for a headline of six words or fewer.

proposals.name: Colon-led topic label
proposals.instruction: DESCRIPTION: Begins with a short label followed by a colon and a proposition.

proposals.name: Interrogative packaging
proposals.instruction: DESCRIPTION: Begins with “how,” “why,” “what,” “will,” or “can” and poses a question.

proposals.name: Promotion or media tag
proposals.instruction: DESCRIPTION: Contains a label such as “live,” “watch,” “video,” “explained,” or “in pictures.”

proposals.name: Continuation or sequence cue
proposals.instruction: DESCRIPTION: Explicitly signals sequence or continuation, such as “day 18,” “still,” “again,” or “what now.”

proposals.name: Calendar or daypart wording
proposals.instruction: DESCRIPTION: Names a weekday, holiday, season, date, or time of day.

proposals.name: Wire-style attribution syntax
proposals.instruction: DESCRIPTION: Uses source-first wording such as “police say,” “X says,” or “boss warns.”

proposals.name: Acronym-heavy casing
proposals.instruction: DESCRIPTION: Contains at least two all-uppercase abbreviations, such as “US,” “UN,” or “DR.”

proposals.name: Scare-quote packaging
proposals.instruction: DESCRIPTION: Places a single evaluative word or short phrase in quotation marks without presenting a full quotation.

proposals.name: First-person or plea framing
proposals.instruction: DESCRIPTION: Uses “I,” “we,” “me,” or “my,” or directly frames a personal plea.

proposals.name: Immediate Clarity
proposals.instruction: Scores high when the headline clearly identifies who did what and why; low when elliptical, vague, or metaphorical. Does not apply when the wording provides no recoverable event structure.
proposals.rationale: Clear headlines reduce comprehension costs and make clicking more likely.

proposals.name: Curiosity Gap
proposals.instruction: Scores high when the headline withholds a salient answer while implying one exists; low when it fully resolves the story or supplies no hook. Does not apply without an implied unanswered question.
proposals.rationale: Unresolved information can motivate readers to click for completion.

proposals.name: Emotional Language
proposals.instruction: Scores high when wording explicitly conveys fear, outrage, wonder, shame, grief, or delight; low when emotionally neutral. Does not apply when affect is supplied only by the underlying event category.
proposals.rationale: Explicit emotion can attract attention beyond institutional or event severity.

proposals.name: Personal Actionability
proposals.instruction: Scores high when the headline suggests information useful for an individual decision or behavior; low when no personal response is imaginable. Does not apply without a plausible reader-facing action or implication.
proposals.rationale: Practical utility can drive readership independently of domestic relevance.

proposals.name: Moral Identity Contest
proposals.instruction: Scores high when the headline challenges a group identity, taboo, or moral norm; low when it merely describes facts. Does not apply when no value-laden identity or norm is invoked.
proposals.rationale: Identity-relevant disagreement can generate strong reader motivation and discussion.

proposals.name: First-Person Disclosure
proposals.instruction: Scores high when a quoted speaker reveals personal experience, feeling, motive, or confession; low when no intimate voice appears. Does not apply when quotation is only an official factual statement.
proposals.rationale: Personal disclosure creates immediacy distinct from generic human-interest content.

proposals.name: Visual Vividness
proposals.instruction: Scores high when the words evoke a concrete, easily pictured scene, object, or action; low when abstract or bureaucratic. Does not apply when the headline contains no imageable content.
proposals.rationale: Vivid mental imagery can increase attention and memorability.

proposals.name: Goal Conflict
proposals.instruction: Scores high when opposing parties, positions, or objectives are explicitly juxtaposed; low when the headline presents one-sided activity. Does not apply when no competing aims or claims are stated.
proposals.rationale: Interpersonal or ideological contest can attract clicks without requiring crisis or violence.

proposals.name: Expectation Reversal
proposals.instruction: Scores high when the headline signals an outcome contrary to an apparent expectation, especially through reversal or contradiction. Does not apply when no expectation can be inferred from the wording.
proposals.rationale: Structural surprise may engage readers beyond ordinary novelty.

proposals.name: Future Uncertainty
proposals.instruction: Scores high when the headline foregrounds an unresolved consequence, conditional future, or “what happens next” problem; low when the outcome is settled. Does not apply when no future state is implicated.
proposals.rationale: Uncertain consequences can sustain reader interest independently of current crisis.

proposals.name: Verification Cue
proposals.instruction: Scores high when the headline references footage, records, data, fact-checking, testimony, or another evidentiary basis; low when it presents an unsupported assertion. Does not apply when no evidence or sourcing cue appears.
proposals.rationale: Credibility signals can make a claim worth investigating.

proposals.name: Semantic Accessibility
proposals.instruction: Scores high when ordinary vocabulary and familiar references permit understanding without specialist knowledge; low when jargon or obscure terminology dominates. Does not apply when accessibility cannot be judged from the headline alone.
proposals.rationale: Accessible wording broadens the potential readership beyond topic specialists.

proposals.name: Cultural Resonance
proposals.instruction: Scores high when the headline invokes a widely shared cultural text, ritual, symbol, or historical reference; low when culturally unanchored. Does not apply when no shared cultural cue is present.
proposals.rationale: Shared references can create recognition and personal relevance without relying on celebrity.

proposals.name: Consequence Specificity
proposals.instruction: Scores high when the headline states a concrete result, change, or implication; low when it uses generic verbs such as “warns” or “faces pressure.” Does not apply when no consequence is asserted or implied.
proposals.rationale: Specific consequences help readers judge why the story matters.

proposals.name: Conversation Potential
proposals.instruction: Scores high when the headline presents a compact, quotable claim likely to invite agreement, disagreement, or sharing; low when it is routine and non-evaluative. Does not apply without a proposition or viewpoint to react to.
proposals.rationale: Anticipated discussion can increase readership independently of listed news values.

proposals.name: Headline length
proposals.instruction: DESCRIPTION: Count words and clauses; unusually compressed or expansive headlines may reflect slot space, not reader appeal.

proposals.name: Interrogative framing
proposals.instruction: DESCRIPTION: Flag headlines framed as a question or beginning with “How,” “Why,” or “What.” This may reflect explainer packaging rather than underlying readership merit.

proposals.name: Quoted first-person voice
proposals.instruction: DESCRIPTION: Flag a first-person statement or direct personal quotation, especially with an “I” construction. This can identify interview or feature packaging independent of article appeal.

proposals.name: Teaser punctuation
proposals.instruction: DESCRIPTION: Flag quotation marks around vague or evaluative words, ellipses, dashes, or other teaser-like punctuation. Such formatting may be a house-style or curiosity device.

proposals.name: Place-name density
proposals.instruction: DESCRIPTION: Count explicit countries, cities, regions, or demonyms in the headline. Geographic density may reveal assignment desk or bureau origin rather than readership merit.

proposals.name: Legal-procedural diction
proposals.instruction: DESCRIPTION: Flag terms such as “court,” “arrest,” “ruling,” “trial,” “accused,” or “guilty.” These may proxy the legal or crime beat.

proposals.name: Political office titles
proposals.instruction: DESCRIPTION: Count formal political or institutional titles such as president, PM, senator, or congressman. This may reflect politics-desk production and packaging.
proposals.upstream_parent: politics desk and political news cycle

proposals.name: Human-interest vocabulary
proposals.instruction: DESCRIPTION: Flag family, child, grandmother, plea, personal revelation, or similarly intimate wording. Such wording may identify feature-desk staffing or a soft-news template.

proposals.name: Running-story continuity cues
proposals.instruction: DESCRIPTION: Flag “still,” “again,” “day N,” “what now,” or other wording that presupposes an earlier story. These cues may encode persistence in a multi-day news run.

proposals.name: Wire-copy boilerplate
proposals.instruction: DESCRIPTION: Flag formulaic constructions such as “X says,” “X denies,” “X to visit,” or “X found at Y,” with minimal descriptive variation. This may identify syndicated or routine desk copy.

proposals.name: IMMEDIATE COMPREHENSIBILITY
proposals.instruction: Scores high when wording is instantly understandable on first reading, and low when syntax or vocabulary requires rereading. Does not apply when the headline is too fragmentary to judge.
proposals.rationale: Lower processing effort makes a headline more likely to convert homepage exposure into a click.

proposals.name: CONCRETE SPECIFICITY
proposals.instruction: Scores high when the headline names specific actors, actions, objects, places, or numbers, and low when it relies on generic abstractions. Does not apply when semantic content is insufficient.
proposals.rationale: Specific details help readers assess relevance and distinguish compelling stories from generic news.

proposals.name: CURIOSITY GAP
proposals.instruction: Scores high when a concrete question or outcome is deliberately left unresolved, and low when the headline fully resolves the central question or is merely vague. Does not apply without an implied information gap.
proposals.rationale: A bounded information gap creates a reason to open the article.

proposals.name: EXPLANATORY PAYOFF
proposals.instruction: Scores high when the headline promises causes, meaning, or implications, and low when it merely announces an event. Does not apply when no apparent explanatory question exists.
proposals.rationale: Readers click when the headline promises understanding, not merely another event notice.

proposals.name: PERSONAL SELF-RELEVANCE
proposals.instruction: Scores high when ordinary readers can readily connect the topic to their own lives, and low when relevance is remote or specialized. Does not apply when the headline gives no basis for judging audience relevance.
proposals.rationale: Perceived personal relevance is a direct motivation for readership.

proposals.name: EMOTIONAL VIVIDNESS
proposals.instruction: Scores high when wording or circumstances evoke a strong feeling beyond formal crisis or violence, and low when affect is flat or purely administrative. Does not apply to emotionally neutral wording.
proposals.rationale: Affective activation can attract attention beyond formal news-value signals.

proposals.name: IDENTITY RESONANCE
proposals.instruction: Scores high when the headline invokes a recognizable social, national, political, religious, or generational identity with value stakes, and low when no identity is salient. Does not apply when relevant identities are unstated.
proposals.rationale: Group-linked stakes can mobilize readership without elite actors or domestic relevance.

proposals.name: MORAL EVALUATION
proposals.instruction: Scores high when the headline clearly signals wrongdoing, injustice, betrayal, vindication, compassion, or admiration, and low when it is morally neutral. Does not apply when judgment derives only from legal status or violence.
proposals.rationale: Clear moral meaning can trigger interest, judgment, and sharing.

proposals.name: NARRATIVE TENSION
proposals.instruction: Scores high when identifiable goals, obstacles, or opposing forces remain unresolved, and low when the headline describes a static or completed state. Does not apply without discernible actors or objectives.
proposals.rationale: Unresolved goals and obstacles invite readers to learn what happens next.

proposals.name: PRACTICAL UTILITY
proposals.instruction: Scores high when the article appears likely to inform a decision, action, precaution, or behavior, and low when it offers no usable implication. Does not apply when no decision-relevant consequence is suggested.
proposals.rationale: Actionable implications give readers a concrete reason to seek more information.

proposals.name: EVIDENCE CUES
proposals.instruction: Scores high when the headline signals footage, records, fact-checking, data, or credible attribution, and low when it presents an unsupported assertion. Does not apply when evidence is irrelevant to the claim.
proposals.rationale: Verification cues increase trust and interest in checking the underlying story.

proposals.name: ACCOUNTABILITY CLARITY
proposals.instruction: Scores high when a specific actor is clearly linked to an action and consequence, and low when responsibility is passive, anonymous, or diffuse. Does not apply when the story involves no assignable responsibility.
proposals.rationale: Clear responsibility makes consequences easier to understand and follow.

proposals.name: VISUAL SCENEABILITY
proposals.instruction: Scores high when the wording readily evokes a concrete, imaginable scene, and low when it remains abstract or conceptual. Does not apply when the subject cannot plausibly be visualized from the headline.
proposals.rationale: Easy-to-imagine scenes improve salience and memorability on a crowded homepage.

proposals.name: CONTEXT INDEPENDENCE
proposals.instruction: Scores high when the headline is intelligible without prior knowledge, and low when it depends on unexplained references or earlier coverage. Does not apply when necessary context is explicitly supplied.
proposals.rationale: Standalone intelligibility prevents prior-story knowledge from becoming a click prerequisite.

proposals.name: PERSONAL AGENCY
proposals.instruction: Scores high when an identifiable individual makes an unusual choice, refusal, admission, or appeal with consequences, and low when individuals are merely mentioned. Does not apply when no individual agency is expressed.
proposals.rationale: Individual choice and consequence create a compact, legible narrative hook.

proposals.name: Headline brevity
proposals.instruction: Count whether the headline is unusually short or compressed, excluding spaces and punctuation.

proposals.name: Template punctuation
proposals.instruction: Mark headlines using a colon, dash, question mark, or quoted phrase in a recognizable house-style template.

proposals.name: Explainer framing
proposals.instruction: Mark “why,” “how,” “what now,” or similarly explicit explanatory framing.

proposals.name: Celebrity-name anchor
proposals.instruction: Mark a headline centered on a named entertainer, athlete, or other celebrity.

proposals.name: Domestic shorthand
proposals.instruction: Mark UK-audience shorthand such as “PM,” “UK,” or locally familiar institutional references.

proposals.name: International-place density
proposals.instruction: Count prominent foreign countries, cities, or regions named in the headline.
proposals.upstream_parent: International desk, time zone, or correspondent availability

proposals.name: Running-story marker
proposals.instruction: Mark explicit continuation cues such as “still,” “again,” “day 18,” “after,” or “what now.”

proposals.name: Calendar-era vocabulary
proposals.instruction: Mark references to Covid, Christmas, elections, or other calendar-specific events that date the headline.

proposals.name: Interview-voice quotation
proposals.instruction: Mark a headline built around a first-person statement or a distinctive person’s quoted words.

proposals.name: Colloquial sensational wording
proposals.instruction: Mark conspicuously vivid, playful, emotional, or conversational wording rather than neutral description.

proposals.name: Concrete information gap
proposals.instruction: Score high when the headline poses or implies a specific unanswered question a click could resolve; score low when it gives a complete, settled account. Do not apply when no meaningful question is inferable.
proposals.rationale: Unresolved questions create a direct click motive without depending on editorial prominence.

proposals.name: Outcome or resolution payoff
proposals.instruction: Score high when the headline states a discovery, verdict, rescue, cancellation, or other consequential outcome; score low when no result is provided. Do not apply when no event outcome is described.
proposals.rationale: Readers may click to obtain closure, even when the topic lacks classic news value.

proposals.name: Evidence or reveal cue
proposals.instruction: Score high when the headline promises hidden evidence, verification, admission, or a newly uncovered record; score low when it merely asserts a position. Do not apply when no disclosure or evidence cue appears.
proposals.rationale: Reveals and verification offer informational value beyond ordinary event reporting.

proposals.name: Explicit causal linkage
proposals.instruction: Score high when the headline clearly states why one event produces another; score low when it merely juxtaposes facts. Do not apply when causation is not central to the story.
proposals.rationale: Causal coherence helps readers understand why an event matters and motivates explanatory clicks.

proposals.name: Concrete scene imagery
proposals.instruction: Score high when the headline depicts a specific action, place, object, or observable scene; score low when it uses only abstract concepts. Do not apply when no scene detail is present.
proposals.rationale: Vivid imagery makes unfamiliar stories mentally accessible and memorable.

proposals.name: Self-contained context
proposals.instruction: Score high when the headline identifies enough actors, events, and circumstances to understand its premise; score low when it depends on unexplained references or prior coverage. Do not apply when contextual sufficiency cannot be judged.
proposals.rationale: Self-contained headlines reduce comprehension costs for broad same-site readership.

proposals.name: Plain-language accessibility
proposals.instruction: Score high when wording is familiar, direct, and syntactically simple; score low when it relies on jargon, convoluted syntax, or obscure references. Do not apply when specialized terminology is unavoidable and clearly explained.
proposals.rationale: Accessibility increases the number of readers who can immediately understand the click proposition.

proposals.name: Practical personal utility
proposals.instruction: Score high when the headline implies usable consequences for personal safety, rights, health, travel, or finances; score low when no personal decision is suggested. Do not apply when reader action is not inferable.
proposals.rationale: Direct usefulness can drive readership independently of economic impact or domestic relevance.

proposals.name: First-hand testimony
proposals.instruction: Score high when an affected person gives a first-person account, plea, or disclosure; score low when the headline offers only an impersonal summary. Do not apply when the quotation is merely an official position.
proposals.rationale: First-hand voice can create identification and trust beyond generic human-interest framing.

proposals.name: Explicit interpersonal clash
proposals.instruction: Score high when named people or groups directly disagree, accuse, reject, or challenge one another; score low when only one position appears. Do not apply when disagreement is merely inferred.
proposals.rationale: Legible conflict supplies narrative tension without requiring violence, crisis, or legal proceedings.

proposals.name: Expectation reversal
proposals.instruction: Score high when wording signals a contradiction or reversal against an implied expectation, such as “despite,” “still,” or “but”; score low for straightforward developments. Do not apply when no baseline expectation is visible.
proposals.rationale: Reversals create cognitive tension that can attract clicks independently of general novelty.

proposals.name: Consequential uncertainty
proposals.instruction: Score high when future or conditional wording is paired with a specified possible consequence; score low for forecasts without meaningful stakes. Do not apply when no future contingency is present.
proposals.rationale: Uncertainty with stakes encourages monitoring behavior beyond generic recency.

proposals.name: Emotional immediacy
proposals.instruction: Score high when the headline contains an explicit plea, fear, grief, anger, shame, or other strong affect; score low when emotionally neutral. Do not apply when emotional wording is incidental.
proposals.rationale: Immediate affect can trigger attention without requiring celebrity, violence, or human-interest framing.

proposals.name: Memorable verbal packaging
proposals.instruction: Score high when an understandable idiom, metaphor, pun, or striking phrase makes the headline distinctive; score low for boilerplate wording. Do not apply when no salient phrasing appears.
proposals.rationale: Memorable language helps a headline stand out among competing stories.

proposals.name: Local specificity plus universal stakes
proposals.instruction: Score high when a concrete person or place is paired with a clearly general human consequence; score low when either element is absent. Do not apply when neither level is visible.
proposals.rationale: Concrete entry points combined with broad relevance can expand readership beyond directly affected audiences.

proposals.name: Headline length
proposals.instruction: DESCRIPTION: Count the headline’s words; unusually short or long headlines form a measurable format proxy.

proposals.name: Quotation-mark framing
proposals.instruction: DESCRIPTION: Mark whether the headline contains quoted speech or scare quotes.

proposals.name: Question or explainer form
proposals.instruction: DESCRIPTION: Mark headlines phrased as questions or explicit “what/why/how” explainers.

proposals.name: Curiosity-gap wording
proposals.instruction: DESCRIPTION: Mark headlines that withhold the central referent or outcome, using vague hooks such as “what now,” “episode,” or “two parts.”

proposals.name: Named-person lead
proposals.instruction: DESCRIPTION: Mark headlines beginning with a specific person’s name, title, or celebrity identity.

proposals.name: Institutional-action boilerplate
proposals.instruction: DESCRIPTION: Mark formulaic constructions such as “court blocks,” “president says,” “UN urges,” or “police find.”

proposals.name: International place-name density
proposals.instruction: DESCRIPTION: Count countries, cities, regions, or demonyms appearing in the headline, especially multiple such references.

proposals.name: Numerals and scale quantifiers
proposals.instruction: DESCRIPTION: Mark digits, ordinals, and terms such as “hundreds,” “thousands,” “largest,” or “top.”

proposals.name: Personal and emotional framing
proposals.instruction: DESCRIPTION: Mark kinship terms, pleas, first-person testimony, vulnerability, or strongly affective adjectives.

proposals.name: Running-story installment markers
proposals.instruction: DESCRIPTION: Mark explicit continuation cues such as “day 18,” “still,” “after,” “remains,” or “what now.”
proposals.upstream_parent: story age and position in a multi-day news run

proposals.name: Direct Audience Addressing
proposals.instruction: Headlines using first or second person pronouns (I, we, you) score high; third-person or objective headlines score low.
proposals.rationale: Personal pronouns forge an immediate psychological connection, strongly driving reader click-through rates.

proposals.name: Clickbait Information Gap
proposals.instruction: Headlines framing a mystery or withheld revelation (e.g., "What happened", "Why") score high; explicit factual statements score low.
proposals.rationale: Exploiting the curiosity gap heavily incentivizes readers to click to resolve uncertainty.

proposals.name: Narrative Suspense Phrasing
proposals.instruction: Headlines using delayed reveals or cliffhanger syntax (e.g., "felt like an earthquake") score high; fully resolved statements score low.
proposals.rationale: Emotional suspense creates a powerful urge to click and uncover the missing context.

proposals.name: Subjectively Vague Subject
proposals.instruction: Headlines lacking a specific named entity but using emotive nouns (e.g., "Collapse") score high; precise, comprehensive subjects score low.
proposals.rationale: Vague but alarming nouns entice users to click for clarifying specifics not provided upfront.

proposals.name: Identity Politics Conflict
proposals.instruction: Headlines highlighting progressive versus conservative cultural disputes (e.g., abortion, gays, guns) score high; neutral policy headlines score low.
proposals.rationale: Readers frequently click on polarizing cultural issues that resonate with their personal identity.

proposals.name: Viral Digital Scams
proposals.instruction: Headlines mentioning hacking, online scams, or internet security flaws score high; physical infrastructure failures score low.
proposals.rationale: Readers engage heavily with personal digital security threats and viral internet phenomena.

proposals.name: Bizarre Juxtaposition
proposals.instruction: Headlines combining unlikely concepts (e.g., "Congressman" and "comic") score high; traditional institutional pairings score low.
proposals.rationale: Absurd or highly unusual combinations trigger intense curiosity, boosting user clicks.

proposals.name: Child Vulnerability Hook
proposals.instruction: Headlines centering on the peril, exploitation, or targeting of a child score high; adult-focused vulnerability headlines score low.
proposals.rationale: Evolutionary psychology makes threats to children highly salient, driving immediate reader engagement.

proposals.name: Hard News Geography Overload
proposals.instruction: Headlines naming multiple non-Western regions or complex foreign conflicts score low; domestic or single-named regions score high.
proposals.rationale: Cognitive load from multiple foreign names reduces casual reader interest and click-through rates.

proposals.name: Localized Impact Framing
proposals.instruction: Headlines framing foreign or political issues through a direct, everyday lens (e.g., "your security") score high; abstract political analysis scores low.
proposals.rationale: Readers click more often when an issue is framed as affecting their daily life directly.

proposals.name: Visual Secret Evidence
proposals.instruction: Headlines explicitly mentioning hidden or leaked footage score high; standard investigative reports or summaries score low.
proposals.rationale: The promise of viewing exclusive, illicit, or visual proof is a powerful click driver.

proposals.name: Technological Disruption
proposals.instruction: Headlines focusing on cryptocurrency, app-based services, or digital disruption score high; traditional corporate earnings score low.
proposals.rationale: Tech and crypto stories draw high engagement from young, digitally native news consumers.

proposals.name: Direct Impact Warning
proposals.instruction: Headlines predicting imminent disaster or mass societal disruption (e.g., "new threat") score high; past-tense analytical stories score low.
proposals.rationale: Future threats create urgency, compelling users to click to ensure their own awareness.

proposals.name: Outgroup Antagonism
proposals.instruction: Headlines highlighting ideological resistance or mocking of elites (e.g., "takes swipe") score high; polite institutional discourse scores low.
proposals.rationale: Readers engage strongly with conflict and stories validating their grievances against political opponents.

proposals.name: Medical Maltreatment
proposals.instruction: Headlines emphasizing botched healthcare, wrong results, or medical testing failures score high; standard policy health news scores low.
proposals.rationale: Institutional medical failures trigger deep personal anxieties, prompting immediate reader investigation.

proposals.name: Story sequence marker
proposals.instruction: Headline starts with a temporal day-count (e.g., "day 18") or references ongoing continuity (e.g., "what now for").

proposals.name: Continuing news verb
proposals.instruction: Uses verbs indicating ongoing evolution rather than a discrete event (e.g., "remains," "takes shine off").

proposals.name: Reader-roadmap interrogative
proposals.instruction: Formatted as a forward-looking question starting with "How," "Why," or "What."

proposals.name: Punchy single quote marker
proposals.instruction: Headline features a brief, sensational single quote (e.g., 'unacceptable', 'colossal').

proposals.name: Exceptionalism framing device
proposals.instruction: Uses specific phrasing to highlight stark contrast or irony (e.g., "despite," "but," "still").

proposals.name: Appositive name emphasis
proposals.instruction: Places a subject's name before a colon to introduce a personal quote or revelation (e.g., "Harry:", "Robinhood boss:").

proposals.name: Regional geopolitics lexicon
proposals.instruction: Highlights institutional actions in non-Western regions using terms like "court blocks," "urged to," or "backs."

proposals.name: Syndicated feature syntax
proposals.instruction: Uses colloquial idioms or slang (e.g., "wrong 'un," "takes swipe") indicating a softer human interest feature.

proposals.name: Entanglement booster phrase
proposals.instruction: Includes text explicitly linking separate major news cycles or topics (e.g., "Coronavirus halts...").

proposals.name: Bureaucratic event marker
proposals.instruction: References abstract institutional processes without named individuals (e.g., "Georgia voter fraud claims").

proposals.name: High-recognition celebrity or named individual
proposals.instruction: Scores high if the headline names a globally recognizable celebrity, royal, or prominent individual. Scores low if the subjects are only foreign officials or unknown civilians.
proposals.rationale: Readers exhibit strong click bias toward highly recognizable, famous personalities over institutional actors.

proposals.name: Direct quotation or sensational first-person claim
proposals.instruction: Scores high if the headline features a direct quote or first-person confession. Scores low if it is a standard third-person report.
proposals.rationale: Direct quotes create intimate curiosity and promise exclusive personal details, driving higher reader clicks.

proposals.name: UK-centric novelty or quirky local event
proposals.instruction: Scores high for distinctly British cultural events, local quirks, or unusual domestic community stories. Scores low for foreign affairs or broad global trends.
proposals.rationale: The BBC's domestic audience heavily clicks on relatable, idiosyncratic local news over serious foreign politics.

proposals.name: Recreational internet or tech controversy
proposals.instruction: Scores high if the text references social media, viral memes, streaming platforms, or internet culture. Scores low for traditional politics or hardware.
proposals.rationale: Digital native readers disproportionately click on stories about the platforms and cultural debates they use daily.

proposals.name: Bizarre visual premise or absurd literal claim
proposals.instruction: Scores high if the text explicitly describes a visually absurd, comical, or physically unusual situation. Scores low for standard diplomatic or legal actions.
proposals.rationale: Audiences click absurd or bizarre literal headlines for entertainment and shock value, seeking visual confirmation.

proposals.name: Graphic body violation or visceral violence
proposals.instruction: Scores high if the text contains visceral, graphic bodily terms like rape, caning, or trafficking. Scores low for bloodless institutional violence like 'sanctions' or 'truce fails'.
proposals.rationale: Visceral violence or bodily violation triggers strong morbid curiosity, sparking more reader clicks than abstract institutional events.

proposals.name: Unresolved curiosity gap or implied question
proposals.instruction: Scores high if the headline teases a mystery, a hidden secret, or a rhetorical question without revealing the core fact. Scores low for explicit, complete factual summaries.
proposals.rationale: Omitting key information creates a knowledge gap that heavily incentivizes the reader to click to resolve.

proposals.name: Geopolitical complexity or foreign diplomatic process
proposals.instruction: Scores high for dense foreign diplomacy, distant institutional elections, and complex regional history. Scores low for domestic or personality-driven news.
proposals.rationale: General readers often bypass complex geopolitical processes in favor of simpler, more relatable narratives.

proposals.name: Pop-culture nostalgia or retro media reference
proposals.instruction: Scores high if the headline references retro pop culture, classic media, or past decades. Scores low for current affairs or breaking news.
proposals.rationale: Readers click nostalgia-triggering headlines to relive shared cultural touchstones from their youth.

proposals.name: Ominous but vague future threat
proposals.instruction: Scores high if the headline warns of an impending but undefined crisis or 'national security threat'. Scores low for resolved events or specific facts.
proposals.rationale: Vague future threats create anxiety and curiosity, compelling readers to click to assess their personal risk.

proposals.name: Resolved past event or historical flashback
proposals.instruction: Scores high for articles explaining past conflicts, historical territorial anomalies, or retrospective obituaries. Scores low for breaking or ongoing current events.
proposals.rationale: Readers seeking immediate news click less on historical analyses or retrospective contexts than on active stories.

proposals.name: Consumer tech or everyday product hack
proposals.instruction: Scores high if the text highlights a flaw or hack in a recognizable consumer product. Scores low for macroeconomics or industrial policy.
proposals.rationale: Everyday product vulnerabilities are highly clickable because they immediately impact the reader's personal security or property.

proposals.name: High-emotion adversity or emotional family plea
proposals.instruction: Scores high if the headline focuses on family grief, pleading, or profound personal tragedy. Scores low for abstract policy impacts.
proposals.rationale: Emotional human-interest stories about familial suffering or pleas drive strong empathetic clicking behavior.

proposals.name: Directly contradictory or unexpected juxtaposition
proposals.instruction: Scores high if the headline features an ironic clash of concepts, like Catholic Malta and gay marriage. Scores low for expected, routine pairings.
proposals.rationale: Readers click unexpected juxtapositions seeking to understand how the apparent contradiction logically resolves.

proposals.name: Unintuitive causal mechanism or systemic failure
proposals.instruction: Scores high if a systemic action causes an unintended, dramatic real-world side effect. Scores low for predictable political outcomes.
proposals.rationale: Bizarre real-world consequences of policies intrigue readers by violating normal expectations of institutional logic.

proposals.name: Named US elite actor present
proposals.instruction: Headline explicitly names a current or former US politician, government institution, or major US law enforcement agency.

proposals.name: Active Anglophone celebrity quoted
proposals.instruction: Headline centers on a well-known English-speaking entertainment or pop-culture figure, often using quotation marks for their speech.

proposals.name: Named foreign geopolitical conflict zone
proposals.instruction: Headline references ongoing unrest in a non-Anglophone country, often combining a geographic proper noun with institutional or military terms.

proposals.name: UK domestic life disrupted by policy
proposals.instruction: Headline text describes a logistical, legal, or economic restriction affecting daily civilian life in the UK.

proposals.name: Quirky or oddity human-interest phrasing
proposals.instruction: Headline uses colloquialisms, puns, or eccentric framing for a non-hard-news event.

proposals.name: Running story day-count tag
proposals.instruction: Headline text contains ordinal day numbers or explicit references to being part of an ongoing multi-day story.

proposals.name: Headline takes analytical question form
proposals.instruction: Headline is formatted entirely or primarily as a question meant to explain a complex issue.

proposals.name: Headline takes feature analysis form
proposals.instruction: Headline begins with "Why", "How", or "What" to signal a long-form background analysis rather than breaking news.

proposals.name: Named region plus institutional action
proposals.instruction: Headline pairs a specific geographic location (often a developing nation) with formal verbs like urges, blocks, or delays.

proposals.name: Explicit mentions of violent victimization
proposals.instruction: Headline contains specific violent or sexual crime keywords like rape, killed, or trafficked.

proposals.name: Quoted Colloquialism
proposals.instruction: Headlines using informal, idiomatic, or slang phrasing in quotes score high (e.g., "wrong 'un"). Formal headlines score low. Does not apply to straight news quotes.
proposals.rationale: Casual phrasing drives curiosity and signals lighthearted, highly clickable content.

proposals.name: Implicit Mystery Gap
proposals.instruction: Headlines deliberately omitting key information (e.g., "smack a space rock") score high. Headlines stating all facts clearly score low.
proposals.rationale: Withholding the main subject creates a curiosity gap that directly forces reader clicks.

proposals.name: Prominent Western Elite Actor
proposals.instruction: Headlines featuring globally recognized Western politicians/celebrities score high. Unknown or non-Western figures score low. Does not apply to generic institutions.
proposals.rationale: BBC's domestic audience disproportionately clicks on highly familiar Western cultural figures.

proposals.name: Localized Geographic Exoticism
proposals.instruction: Headlines framed as questions about unusual specific locations (e.g., "two parts of Africa") score high. Standard geopolitical news scores low.
proposals.rationale: Explainer formats about unfamiliar places leverage high curiosity and broad general appeal.

proposals.name: Fronted Question Interrogative
proposals.instruction: Headlines starting with "What", "How", or "Why" score high if they promise a direct explanation. Statements score low. Does not apply to rhetorical quotes.
proposals.rationale: Question headlines explicitly promise to resolve an information gap, strongly motivating reader clicks.

proposals.name: UK/Domestic Cultural Anchor
proposals.instruction: Headlines featuring exclusively UK-centric personalities/events (e.g., Grenfell, Stormzy) score high. Foreign events score low. Does not apply to generic foreign policy.
proposals.rationale: The BBC's primary demographic clicks heavily on domestic cultural touchstones and local outrage.

proposals.name: Playful Alliteration or Pun
proposals.instruction: Headlines with obvious wordplay (e.g., "hot tub hack") score high. Straightforward factual headlines score low. Does not apply to serious tragedies.
proposals.rationale: Linguistic playfulness signals a softer, entertaining read, which drives high impulse clicks.

proposals.name: Hyperbolic Evaluative Adjective
proposals.instruction: Headlines using strong subjective adjectives like "amazing", "colossal", or "unacceptable" score high. Neutral adjectives score low.
proposals.rationale: Hyperbole amplifies emotional arousal and perceived stakes, prompting immediate reader investigation.

proposals.name: Lack of Public Policy Jargon
proposals.instruction: Headlines avoiding complex political/institutional terms (e.g., "borrowing", "pact") score high. Jargon-heavy headlines score low.
proposals.rationale: Casual readers bypass complex policy headlines, preferring accessible, human-centric daily stories.

proposals.name: Imminent Ongoing Temporality
proposals.instruction: Headlines referencing an event actively unfolding or launching (e.g., "set for launch") score high. Past or historical events score low.
proposals.rationale: Readers prioritize clicking on dynamic, real-time events to stay updated on breaking news.

proposals.name: Bizarre Novelty Contrast
proposals.instruction: Headlines combining two unexpected elements (e.g., "oath on a comic") score high. Expected pairings score low.
proposals.rationale: Juxtaposing normal institutional actions with absurd props creates massive cognitive dissonance and clicks.

proposals.name: Named Western Outlets/Brands
proposals.instruction: Headlines featuring recognizable corporate brands (Netflix, Wikipedia, Robinhood) score high. Obscure organizations score low. Does not apply to governments.
proposals.rationale: High familiarity with consumer brands creates immediate personal relevance and triggers reader trust.

proposals.name: Outrage-Inducing Specifier
proposals.instruction: Headlines containing vulnerable victims or shocking crimes (e.g., "stolen ashes") score high. Routine crimes score low.
proposals.rationale: Visceral emotional triggers bypass editorial constraints to elicit strong, immediate reader clicking behavior.

proposals.name: Direct Pronoun Posessive Hook
proposals.instruction: Headlines leading with a first-person quote ("I can tell", "my family") score high. Third-person institutional actions score low.
proposals.rationale: First-person narrative intimacy signals a deeply personal, gossip-level story that drives impulse clicks.

proposals.name: Explicit Visceral Violence Term
proposals.instruction: Headlines featuring direct physical violence words score high. Institutional terms like "fraud" or "infiltration" score low.
proposals.rationale: Readers are psychologically wired to click on explicit physical threats and violent anomalies.

proposals.name: Playful or quirky phrasing
proposals.instruction: Headline uses puns, alliteration, informal verbs, or idiomatic phrases, indicating an editorial push to make a story highly clickable.
proposals.upstream_parent: Editorial curation and audience engagement strategy

proposals.name: Top-tier US political actor
proposals.instruction: Headline explicitly names major US politicians or parties, catching the articulated criteria's elite actor value regardless of UK reader demand.

proposals.name: Strong emotion or outrage markers
proposals.instruction: Headline features highly emotive language (e.g., "troubled", "unacceptable", "snag") or dramatic human tragedy, creating an outsize clickability signal.

proposals.name: Niche historical or cultural framing
proposals.instruction: Headline focuses on historical facts, explanations of borders, or abstract cultural shifts, reflecting explanatory feature writing that gets promoted but isn't urgently clicked.

proposals.name: Broad regional institutional action
proposals.instruction: Headline mentions general geographic regions (e.g., "Africa", "Pacific") or distant institutional conflicts lacking specific elite names, acting as broad foreign news markers.

proposals.name: Discrete geographic country name
proposals.instruction: Headline features the exact name of a single foreign country, triggering domestic relevance and institutional markers without ensuring UK audience interest.
proposals.upstream_parent: Wire copy and foreign desk templates

proposals.name: Direct quote from an actor
proposals.instruction: Headline consists primarily of a dramatic or bold quotation, signaling a soft news interview exclusive that editors feature prominently.
proposals.upstream_parent: PR cycle and daily interview exclusives

proposals.name: Soft news humanization cliché
proposals.instruction: Headline uses tropes like "America's girl next door" or "cycle of pain" signaling a glossy feature profile rather than urgent hard news.
proposals.upstream_parent: Soft news and celebrity desk quotas

proposals.name: Continuing running story label
proposals.instruction: Headline uses explicit day counters or references a ongoing multi-day narrative, marking it as a continuation rather than a novel, standalone event.

proposals.name: Royalty or UK TV celebrity name
proposals.instruction: Headline explicitly names UK royalty or personalities from popular British television, highly clickable to local audiences but undervalued by elite political criteria.

proposals.name: PERSONAL REVELATION
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high if headline explicitly describes a celebrity or elite personally revealing a secret, trauma, or taboo. Scores low for routine institutional statements. Does not apply to general news.
proposals.rationale: Readers click intimate psychological confessions by famous people, driving massive same-outlet engagement.

proposals.name: DIRECT ADDRESS OR FIRST-PERSON QUOTE
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high if text uses first-person perspective or quotes someone speaking directly. Scores low for indirect reported speech. Does not apply to unquoted text.
proposals.rationale: Quotes create immediate psychological proximity and urgency, increasing reader interest and subsequent clicks.

proposals.name: VIOLENT OR SEXUAL CRIME ACCUSATION
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high for explicit mentions of violent/sexual charges or acquittals involving named individuals. Scores low for general geopolitical conflict. Does not apply to non-crime news.
proposals.rationale: True crime and sexual scandal carry a strong morbid curiosity factor that reliably drives clicks.

proposals.name: BUZZWORDS AND INTERNET SLANG
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high if headline uses highly informal, viral, or tech-internet slang (e.g., "smack", "hack", "snag"). Scores low for formal diplomatic language. Does not apply to standard journalistic phrasing.
proposals.rationale: Informal, quirky, or tech-adjacent vocabulary signals accessible soft news, boosting reader clicks.

proposals.name: HUMAN VULNERABILITY OF NON-ELITES
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high if ordinary people are victims of bizarre, emotional, or freak events. Scores low for mass statistics or institutional policies. Does not apply to elites.
proposals.rationale: Bizarre emotional tragedies involving ordinary people trigger empathetic curiosity and high read-rates.

proposals.name: MAJOR ONGOING CONFLICT MILESTONE
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high for chronological updates on major, highly salient wars (e.g., Russia-Ukraine). Scores low for isolated conflicts with low domestic relevance. Does not apply to historical conflicts.
proposals.rationale: Highly salient running stories generate daily suspense; readers click chronological updates to track developments.

proposals.name: TABLOID FRAME OR PLAYFUL PUN
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores high for colloquial puns, jokes, or pop-culture references. Scores low for formal headlines. Does not apply to straight hard news reporting.
proposals.rationale: Entertaining, softly worded headlines act as click-magnets by promising a diverting, easily digestible narrative.

proposals.name: FIGUREHEAD NAME PLUS NEUTRAL ACTION
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores low if headline features a famous person doing something routine or institutional. Scores high if doing something deeply personal. Does not apply to non-celebrities.
proposals.rationale: Mere presence of an elite actor is insufficient for clicks; routine institutional actions bore readers.

proposals.name: OBSCURE FOREIGN POLICY MECHANICS
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores low if detailing complex, distant geopolitical treaties or borders. Scores high if featuring recognizable, immediate crises. Does not apply to domestic politics.
proposals.rationale: Readers routinely ignore distant institutional diplomacy in favor of immediate domestic or highly violent crises.

proposals.name: NON-VIOLENT DOMESTIC POLITICAL STATEMENT
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores low for domestic politicians merely giving warnings or making administrative rulings. Scores high for elections or scandals. Does not apply to international relations.
proposals.rationale: Routine political posturing lacks the novelty or stakes necessary to motivate a reader to click.

proposals.name: DOMESTIC ECONOMIC FORECAST OR STATISTIC
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores low for abstract financial updates, borrowing figures, or market warnings. Scores high for personal finance impacts. Does not apply to corporate business news.
proposals.rationale: Readers click economics that immediately affect their wallets, bypassing abstract macroeconomic financial updates.

proposals.name: EXTREME WEATHER OR ENVIRONMENTAL STATISTIC
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores low for slow-moving environmental data or distant climate reports. Scores high for immediate, local disasters. Does not apply to conservation successes.
proposals.rationale: Distant ecological statistics lack the immediate threat level required to trigger high same-outlet readership.

proposals.name: FORMAL LEGAL PROCEDURE DELAY
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores low for routine court procedural delays, continuances, or scheduling. Scores high for final verdicts or dramatic trials. Does not apply to criminal investigations.
proposals.rationale: Readers seek closure and drama in legal stories, largely ignoring intermediate procedural updates.

proposals.name: UNFAMILIAR FOREIGN PROPER NOUN DOMINANCE
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores low if subjects are unfamiliar foreign institutions or non-elite regional figures. Scores high if featuring globally recognized entities. Does not apply to domestic names.
proposals.rationale: Headline alienation occurs when readers lack mental schemas for obscure geopolitical actors, suppressing clicks.

proposals.name: LOW-STAKES CULTURAL HUMAN INTEREST
proposals.instruction: <=8 words | DESCRIPTION: Scores low for niche arts, obscure history, or minor community projects. Scores high for major celebrity entertainment. Does not apply to hard news.
proposals.rationale: Clicks favor broad, easily understood cultural narratives over specialized features requiring high prior knowledge.

proposals.name: Serial story day counter
proposals.instruction: Headline explicitly denotes an ongoing multi-day event via a numbered day or ordinal term.

proposals.name: Literal direct quote marks
proposals.instruction: Headline contains verbatim quotation marks indicating direct speech, opinion, or a subjective descriptor.
proposals.upstream_parent: Editorial preference for soft-news or interview formatting

proposals.name: Casual or sensational colloquialism
proposals.instruction: Uses informal, slang, or highly evocative vocabulary (e.g., "smack," "snag," "wolf") uncommon in standard hard news.

proposals.name: Analytical interrogative format
proposals.instruction: Opens with a question word (e.g., "How," "Why") implying an explanatory or analytical article.
proposals.upstream_parent: Editorial push for evergreen context or analysis pieces

proposals.name: Geographic curiosity framing
proposals.instruction: Uses phrases like "The country that..." or highlights an obscure geographic territory as a curiosity.

proposals.name: Event ordinality or resolution verb
proposals.instruction: Contains explicit language marking a sequence's conclusion or continuation (e.g., "finally," "now," "delays," "remains").
proposals.upstream_parent: Position within a multi-day news cycle

proposals.name: Celebrity hook on hard news
proposals.instruction: Headlines lead strictly with a recognizable entertainment or sports figure to anchor a broader social issue.
proposals.upstream_parent: SEO or cross-platform traffic optimization strategy

proposals.name: Hyper-specific human-interest detail
proposals.instruction: Lead framing relies on idiosyncratic, granular descriptors (e.g., "Canadian grandma," "drive-through") rather than broad stakes.

proposals.name: Puzzling standalone elliptical headline
proposals.instruction: Highly compressed, ambiguous phrasing lacking context (e.g., "Collapse 'felt like an earthquake'").
proposals.upstream_parent: Homepage placement alongside large visual assets

proposals.name: Explicit fact-checking label
proposals.instruction: Contains in-house terminology such as "Fact-checked," "Explained," or "Analysis" to denote article format.
proposals.upstream_parent: Mandated editorial format for disinformation beats
